chapter: Paul Barbarin and his own bands
title: Burnell Santiago as a boogie-woogie pianist
summary: Breaux describes the pianist's gifts, his ear, his win against Earl Hines in a piano contest, and his boogie-woogie style.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Did you ever work with Barnell?
Oh, Lil' Barham jobs. I mean...

Could he play? His bass is alive. He's a boogie-woogie. Yeah, he played a lot of piano. I mean, he was... I'd say just naturally gifted because he couldn't read. But he could... He could improvise so well. And then... Then Barnell had such a keen ear. He could work in anybody's band. And I don't care what kind of modulation you make, he'll change key along with you. Just the same as if he was reading. As a matter of fact, I recall one time, I think it was on the Pelican, when the Pelican was open, that Earl Hines came down and he and Boynell got titled down a piano contest and he gave him a drill. He really was great.
Would you call him Barrel House, Tonk style, or would you say that he played like anybody in particular, or what?

Well, he had... He was another individualist. He had a style of his own. He was more or less on a boogie-woogie style. But he also played some nice blues. And occasionally, he played a pretty nice ballad. But he was really a boogie-woogie piano player. I'd call him that. He was a boogie-woogie man.
Yeah. He had a good two-hand.
